idiom_name: pthread_create + caller-supplied completion callback (or a completion queue drained by the owner)
implementation_notes: The start function allocates a per-call record, spawns a worker with pthread_create and returns immediately; the worker computes the result and delivers completion by invoking the stored callback - or, preferably, by posting the record to a queue or self-pipe that the owner drains, so the callback executes on the owner's thread. This is the manual realization: C has no async syntax, no future type and no dispatcher, so cancellation, progress and the exactly-once guarantee are conventions the API author documents. Prefer the queue form when the caller owns an event loop (post, then dispatch); direct invocation is acceptable when the caller is already a worker pool without an event context.
pitfalls: Invoking the completion on the worker thread while the caller mutates the same data is a race: either post the completion to the caller's queue/self-pipe or hand ownership of the record over explicitly.
pthread_create per operation without join or detach leaks thread resources, and pthread_cancel cannot stop work safely - give the worker a cancellation flag it polls.
The operation record must outlive the worker and be freed exactly once (on completion or cancellation), otherwise the stored callback pointer dangles.

variants.name: POSIX AIO request whose sigevent announces completion
variants.implementation_notes: POSIX AIO is the only standardized completion-notification object C has: the request struct carries aio_sigevent, which specifies the notification that occurs when the request is complete - a signal to the process or the invocation of a function in a new thread - so aio_read/aio_write become the start method and the notification is the event. Implementations differ (glibc emulates AIO with threads, the Linux kernel path is restricted), so treat delivery as platform-specific and keep the same per-call record and cancellation discipline as the manual variant.
pitfalls: SIGEV_THREAD callbacks may run concurrently for several requests and on implementation-created threads, so shared state touched by on_done needs its own locking.
aio_return/aio_error must be read exactly once per request, and buffer plus aiocb must stay valid until completion - a stack-allocated aiocb is the classic dangling-completion bug.
